                               PRICE TRENDS
      Labour Bureau an attached office of Ministry of Labour and Employment, since
      its inception has, inter-alia, been entrusted with the responsibility of compilation,
      maintenance and disseminating of the Consumer Price Index for Industrial
      Workers. The CPI-IW is compiled as per international best practices &
      guidelines of ILO and dissemination of CPI-IW is Special Data Dissemination
      Standard (SDDS) compliant. It is released on last working day of subsequent
      month. CPI (IW) are compiled and released by the Labour Bureau, Ministry of
      Labour and Employment and are specific to population segments.

1.1   Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW), one of the prominent
      economic indicators, which measures the relative changes in retail prices over
      a period of time in respect of a fixed set of goods and services consumed by an
      average working class family in a given area with reference to a base year. The
      CPI-IW is mainly used for regulating and determination of dearness allowance
      (DA) being paid to large number of Central/State Government employees and
      also to the workers in the industrial sectors besides fixation and revision of
      minimum wages in scheduled employments, hence, having significant financial
      implications to the Public Exchequer. Further, CPI numbers are widely used as
      macroeconomic indicator of inflation, and also as a tool by government and
      central banks for targeting inflation and monitoring price stability.

1.2   From the month of September, 2020 the Labour Bureau has updated the Base
      of the old Series of CPI -IW (2001=100) to the New Base 2016=100. The main
      components for constructing Consumer Price Index numbers are the weights
      and prices. Weights are the share of actual expenditure on each commodity
      during the base period and base prices are the annual average of item level
      prices during the 2016 in respect of items retained in the index basket.

1.3   The definition of price adopted for the compilation of CPI is the price which a
      consumer/industrial worker has to pay for the specified item/variety, for the
      specified unit, in the selected shop of the selected market. It includes all taxes
      like sales tax, etc., and excludes rebates and discounts, which are universally
      applicable for all the customers. It is the actual price prevailing in the open
      market at which transaction takes place between a buyer and a seller. The
      Black market or unauthorized prices are, however, not taken in the compilation
      of index numbers. In case of rationed commodities, the fair price is taken.

1.4   Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a reflection of changes in the retail prices of
      specified goods and services over a time period, whereas Wholesale Price
      index (WPI) accounts for changes in the general price level of goods at the

                                                                                         1
 90       ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26
        wholesale level. WPI is the primary measure used for ascertaining inflation as
        it accounts for changes in prices for a given class of goods or services in a given
        region, during a given interval of time. Price Indices have several potential uses.
        The index can be said to measure the movement in prices or a cost of living.

           Some notable price indices are indicated below
      I.      Wholesale Price Index number-All India (WPI)
      II.     Consumer Price Index number for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW)
      III.    Consumer Price Index number for Agricultural Laborers (CPI-AL)
      IV.     Consumer Price Index number for Rural Laborers (CPI-RL)

1.5     The substantial change in prices of essential commodities affects both the
        quantum of production and the pattern of consumption. The change in prices
        also makes an impact on the living conditions of people in general and poor in
        particular. Therefore, it is absolutely essential to keep a constant watch on price
        behavior. Statistically index number of prices measures changes in prices over
        a period of time. The price indices are calculated at the wholesale level as well
        as at the retail level.

1.6     The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is the only general index capturing price
        movement in a comprehensive way and is an indicator of movement in prices
        of commodities in all trade and transactions. It is generally taken as an indicator
        of the rate of inflation in the economy. The current series of WPI reflects the
        change in Wholesale Prices over a period as compared to the base year (2011-
        12=100). The information regarding the year-wise wholesale price index from
        2018-19 to 2024-25 is presented in Table 6.1.

2.      Methodology for Compilation of Whole Sale Price Index

2.1     Wholesale price represents the quoted price of the bulk transaction of a
        commodity generally at the primary stage. The revised (current) series of Index
        Numbers of Wholesale Prices in India with base 2011-12 had replaced the
        hitherto operated WPI with base 2004-05. The current series is calculated on
        the principle of weighted arithmetic mean.

2.2     The Price relatives are calculated as the percentage ratios, which current prices
        bear to those prevailing in the base period. In other words, the price relative for
        each variety/quotation is calculated by dividing the current price by the
        corresponding base period (2011-12) price and multiplying the resulting figure
        by 100. The commodity index is arrived at as the simple arithmetic average of
        the price relatives of varieties/quotations selected for that commodity. The
        indices forthe sub-groups/ groups/ major groups of commodities, in turn, are
        worked out as the weighted arithmetic mean of the indices of the items/ sub-
        groups/ groups falling under their respective heads. Being a representative of
        wholesale trade and transaction and also being available on a weekly basis,
        WPI is conventionally used as an indicator to measure the rate of inflation in


                                                                                         1
                                                   ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26     91
        the economy.

2.4            Larger economic integration has allowed developments in international
        markets to trickle down to all corners of the world. At the same time, such
        integration has allowed developing nations to play ever more important roles
        in global markets.In this regard, the rise in commodity prices during this present
        decade highlights the growing importance of the developing world as its
        demand for food, energy and materials appears to have been fuelling the
        current commodity boom.

2.5     Food price inflation is one of the most talked about issues in the country today.
        The brunt of the same is being felt across India and across all sections of
        society.The farmer or the grower may not be benefited in the ratio of the rise in
        food prices as there are huge imperfections in the market. Demand-supply
        mismatches and inefficient supply mechanisms result in large price spreads
        between the growers and final consumers.

  2.6                  In addition to low production and productivity, the prevailing
        market inefficiencies -lack of coordinated efforts in public procurement, wastage
        due to inadequate storage facilities, etc. have been crucial in allowing food
        prices to rise sharply. The complex causes of the current food and agriculture
        crisis require a comprehensive response. The thrust of government activities is
        to concentrate on improving food production and productivity, increasing

           AGRICULTURE & RURAL DEVELOPMENT
       Agricultural activity in NCT of Delhi is being affected due to rapid urbanization
       and growth in other economic activities of trade & industry.

       The percentage distribution of Gross State Value Added (GSVA) of Delhi at
       2011-12 prices showed a declining trend of agriculture and the allied sector. More
       clearly, the percentage contribution of agriculture sector to GSVA of Delhi at
       current prices reduced from 0.32% in 2023-24 to 0.28% in 2024-25.

2.     Land Use Pattern in Delhi

       The total gross cropped area in Delhi got increased to 47050 hectares in 2024-
       25 which was at 33069 hectares during 2023-24. The estimated gross cropped
       area in 2025-26 is 47040 hectares. The remaining areas of the Delhi are being
       used for various other uses such as non-agricultural purposes, forest, fallow land,
       uncultivable land, etc. The information on land use pattern of Delhi is available
       at Table 7.1.

3.     Crop Intensity

3.1 Crop intensity is an index of agriculture development. It is the percentage ratio of
    gross cropped area to net area sown which refers to raising a number of crops
    from the same field during one agricultural year. The index of crop intensity is
    100 if one crop has been grown in a year and it is 200 if two crops are raised.
    Higher the index, greater is the efficiency of land use. The crop intensity has a
    direct correlation with assured irrigation which enables farmers to go in for
    multiple cropping and use a higher dose of fertilizers and HYV seeds. The
    information regarding the crop intensity of Delhi during the last 15 years is
    presented in Statement 7.1.

4.  Cropping Pattern
4.1 Cropping pattern is the sequential arrangement of crops. Paddy, Jowar (Fodder),
    Bajra and Maize during Kharif and Wheat, Mustard, Barley, Gram crops during
    the Rabi seasons are the major crops in Delhi. The cultivation of vegetables is a
    continuous process throughout the year. The information regarding the area,
    production and yields of some of the selected crops in Delhi during 2024-25 and
    2025-26 is presented in Statement 7.2 and 7.3 respectively.

7.       IRRIGATION IN DELHI

7.1 Irrigation in Delhi mainly depends upon groundwater and partly upon surface
    water. Irrigation from the groundwater is provided through the shallow cavity and
    the deep cavity state tube-wells, whereas surface irrigation provided by way of
    utilizing treated effluent available from existing sewage treatment plants located
    at coronation pillar, Okhla and Keshopur. Water from the Western Yamuna Canal
    system under the control of Haryana Govt. is also utilized for irrigation purpose.

7.2 The information regarding the source-wise irrigation and irrigated area in Delhi
    during the last Ten years is presented in Statement 7.5.

8.         Animal Husbandry

8.1    Livestock is an important component in the agriculture sector which affects the
       development of the economy directly and indirectly. Animal husbandry is the
       occupation which takes care of domestic animals that are used primarily as food
       and food products for protein source. Due to rapid urbanization and limited
       availability of feed/fodder/pasture land in NCT of Delhi, scope of Animal
       Husbandry is decreasing continuously. Delhi has become a consumer state
       wherein Livestock and livestock products are being supplied from other states.
       As per 20th Livestock Census, year 2019, number of livestock has reduced to
       3,07,267 from 3,66,397 in 19th Livestock Census (2012). 21st Livestock census
       has been successfully completed, covering approximately 44.28 lakh households
       across 643 villages/Municipal wards in GNCTD. A total of 1,189 enumerators
       and 100 supervisors were engaged in this exercise. The data of the 21st
       Livestock Census is yet to be published by the GoI. Presently, Animal Husbandry
       Unit is providing Veterinary Healthcare services to the Livestock and companion
       animals through a network of 71 operational Veterinary Hospital / Dispensaries
       and 01 Disease Diagnostic Laboratory.

8.2 The information regarding the livestock Census in Delhi during 2012 and 2019 is
    presented in Statement 7.6.

10.        Autonomous / Grant in Aid Institutions

10.1 Grant in Aid to Delhi Animal Welfare Board (DAWB)

           DAWB being the monitoring/ co-coordinating body for 13 district SPCAs, it will
           extend the financial support to them including the finances. The DAWB is also
           responsible for registration of Pet Shops and Dog breeding & marketing centers
           throughout NCT of Delhi. Further there is also provision for extending the
           financial support to the AWBI/DAWB recognized/ empanelled NGO/Animal
           Welfare Organizations who are practically involved in animal welfare activities.




                                                                                                     1
                                                           ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26     107
10.2   Delhi Society Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA)

       For proper enforcement of Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 and the
       rules framed therein, Delhi Government is running Delhi SPCA at Tis Hazari
       since a long time back. The DSPCA has one Veterinary Hospital with infirmary
       at Tis Hazari where sick / injured and abandoned animals are provided shelters,
       feeding and healthcare. The DSPCA also keeps case property animals. It also
       promotes awareness in public for love and compassion towards animals.

       During 2024–25, a total of 494 challans were issued, 10,581 animals were
       rescued, and 78 vehicles were seized. A total revenue of ₹6,44,020 was
       collected from violators of the Act. In addition, 703 animals were treated in the
       infirmary of Delhi SPCA.

       During the CFY 2025-26 (Upto March, 2026), 64 challans have been issued,
       3,732 animals have been rescued, and 32 vehicles have been seized. A total
       revenue of ₹3,08,320 has been collected from violators of the Act, and 288
       animals have been treated in the infirmary of Delhi SPCA.

       Now, in view of Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Establishment and
       Regulation of Societies for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) Rules, 2001
       and reorganization of 13 revenue districts, 13 District SPCAs, one in each
       revenue district will be reconstituted and By-laws of the district societies will
       be framed accordingly.

11 Gaushala/ Gosadan

       In pursuance of section 10 of the Delhi Agriculture Cattle Preservation Act 1994,
       Gaushalas/ Gausadans were established in year 1995. Presently, four
       Gausadans are functioning namely:-
              (1) Shri Krishana Gausadan, Sultanpur Dabas
              (2) Gopal Gausadan, Harewali
              (3) Dabar Hare Krishna Gausadan, Surhera
              (4) Manav Gausadan, Rewla Khanpur

       These Gaushalas/ Gausadans are operational and 19,221 cows and their
       progeny were maintained during 2024–25. In the current financial year 2025–
       26 (up to December 2025), 20,796 cows and their progeny are being
       maintained therein. Payment of GIA of ₹ 20/- per day per cattle is paid to NGOs
       for the purpose of maintenance of the health of the cattle and for proper feeding,
       watering, shelter etc. of the animals in the Gaushalas/ Gausadans by Govt. of
       NCT of Delhi.

                                      CHAPTER 8

                   ENVIRONMENTAL CONCERNS
1.1   Environment and economy are intricately connected. Resources for the economy
      come from the environment, while economic activity has an impact on the
      environment. Economic development without environmental considerations can
      cause serious environmental damage in turn impairing the quality of life of present
      and future generations.

1.2   The present Government in Delhi treated Environment as a moral responsibility
      by not just taking air pollution as a seasonal crisis, but as a structural challenge
      for which Government has implemented concrete solutions such as e-mobility,
      bio-decomposers, waste-to- energy projects and new dust control equipment’s.
      Further, long term and practical solutions have been adopted to ensure lasting
      impact.

1.3   The problem of pollution in Delhi is dealt by the Government through the domain
      of policy and science. Technology, strict enforcement, public participation and
      long-term investment form the four pillars of this model.

1.4   To tackle air pollution effectively, the Delhi Government has implemented the Air
      Pollution Control Plan 2025, under which 100 Vayu Rakshak (Air Guardians)
      equipped with 35 GPS and CCTV have been deployed across the city. These
      Vayu Rakshak monitor dust pollution and vehicle emissions in real time and
      ensure quick action. Strengthening its commitment to pollution control, the
      Government has implemented various other measures as Clean Delhi, Green
      Delhi is no longer a vision but a measurable transformation.

1.5   Government has taken several steps in the recent past to improve the
      environment condition which includes massive focus on afforestation, installation
      of Anti-Smog Gun at construction sites, deployment of Mechanical Road
      Sweepers (MRS), Water Sprinklers (WS) and Mist Sprays at hotspots, Round the
      clock data-driven air monitoring across Delhi, Strict enforcement with smart
      technology, Reinventing road cleanliness across Delhi, e-mobility &clean energy
      push, implementation of Electric Vehicle Policy, ban on single use plastic, better
      management of solid waste, treatment of waste water, improvement of sewage
      system, stringent industrial emission norms etc.

1.6   Govt. of Delhi has launched an innovative platform for submission of pollution-
      related grievances, which is monitored through the Green War Room called Green
      Delhi App, which is a user-friendly mobile-based app with 30 Government
      departments/ agencies of Delhi on one platform, both for Android and IOS mobile
      phone users.

                                                                                         1
                                                   ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26    111
 1.7     To improve Delhi’s air quality and create an entire supply-chain ecosystem for this
         new segment of vehicles, Delhi Govt. established a policy ‘Delhi Electric Vehicles
         Policy, 2026. The policy aims to strengthen the adoption of electric vehicles and
         the development of supporting infrastructure effective from April, 2026 to March,
         2030.


 1.8     With concerted efforts of departments towards air pollution control, ‘Good days’
         (good/satisfactory/moderate days together) have increased from 159 in 2018 to
         200 in 2025.


 1.9     As per the India State of Forest Report (ISFR), 2023 the total Forest and Tree
         cover of NCT of Delhi has become 25.04% (371.31 Sq. km) of its geographical
         area. The percentage of Forest and Tree cover of Delhi at 25.04% is almost equal
         to national average figure. The Green Cover has increased by 4.89 Sq., km from
         2021 to 2023, which is attributed to increase in Tree Cover. It is pertinent to
         mention that among the seven major mega cities in India, Delhi is the greenest
         city and has largest forest cover of 195.28 Sq. km followed by Mumbai 110.84 Sq.
         km and Bengaluru 89.61 Sq. km (ISFR, 2023).

2.3       Measures Taken to Control Air Pollution in Delhi:

2.3.1  Launch of Air Pollution Mitigation Plan 2025: To mitigate air pollution,
the Government of NCT of Delhi launched the 25-Point Air Pollution Mitigation Plan
2025 on 03.06.2025 for year-round pollution control. Key actions are as follows:




                                                                                      1
 114        ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26
1.         Mitigation of dust pollution from roads and open areas:
        a) Innovation to control Pollution
        b) Sprinkling Water to curb dust
c)      Repairing Roads for Dust Control
2.         Management of Construction and Demolition Waste:
        a) Effective Monitoring of Compliances with C&D project using AI and
           Digital Interventions
        b) Ensuring 100% processing of C&D waste and promoting reuse of
           recycled products
        c) Cleaner Government Construction

3.         Control of Vehicular Pollution:
        a) Getting End-of –Life vehicle out of Delhi
        b) Ensuring entry of cleaner goods vehicles in Delhi
        c) Easier seamless entry in Delhi to Control Pollution
        d) Revamping PUC Centers
        e) Promoting Electric Mobility
        f) Ensuring Cleaner Public Transport
        g) Abating Air Pollution Through Effective Road Traffic Management
        h) Curbing Air Pollution through DG sets
4.         Reducing Waste to Reduce Pollution:
        a) Bio mining of legacy waste
        b) Managing waste
        c) Increasing Waste Processing Capacity to Ensure a Future without
           landfills
        d) Curbing Biomass Burning
5.         Monitoring Pollution for Effectively fight It:
        a) New Monitoring Stations and Equipment,
        b) Re-inventorisation of major and minor air pollution source in all identified
           hotspots in Delhi.
6.         Abating industrial pollution:
        a) Strict Enforcement against pollution industries and
        b) Improving Infrastructure in Industrial Areas
7.         Greening Delhi for healthy Delhi:
        a) Comprehensive Greening Initiative
        b) Regulatory framework for Green Initiative
8.         Converting migration to mass movement:
        a) Public Participation for spreading environmental awareness.

1. Anti-Smog guns on high rise buildings: Anti-Smog Guns on High Rise

                                                                                      1
                                                 ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26   117
Buildings: Directions u/s 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 on mandatory
installation of Anti-Smog Guns on high rise buildings (all commercial complexes,
malls, hotels: having built up area more than 3,000 sq. m. and office buildings and other
institutions (G+5 and above)) has been issued on 29.05.2025. So far 156 Nos of Anti-
Smog Guns installed on identified high rise building.

2. Installation of mist spray/similar system/technology agnostic spraying
system on electric poles/other poles: An administrative order dated 30.04.2025, to
install mist spray/similar system/technology agnostic spraying system on electric
poles/other poles in the central verge along the road stretch in Delhi. Installation in or
around the 13 identified air pollution hotspots in Delhi namely: Okhla, Dwarka, Ashok
Vihar, Bawana, Narela, Mundka, Punjabi Bagh, Wazirpur, Rohini, Vivek Vihar, Anand
Vihar (including Mandoli), RK Puram, Jahangir Puri, is being undertaken in the first
phase on priority basis by PWD, DDA, DSIIDC and DMRC, with other areas also in
pipeline. So far Mist Spray Systems have been installed on 656 electric Poles.

3. Increasing the number of construction and demolition waste collection
sites: MCD, NDMC and DCB already have 106, 25 and 1 Collection Points
respectively where Malba/Debris in small quantities can be dumped by general public.
MCD has identified and developing 19 new Malba Sites.

4.    Directions under EPA for doubling of parking charges: Directions u/s 5 of
the Environment Protection Act, 1986 issued on 04.02.2025 issued to ULBs to Double
existing vehicle parking fee in Delhi upon invoking of Stage III (Severe) and Stage IV
(Severe+) under Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) in Delhi and ensure
implementation of directions at authorized parking sites under their jurisdiction.


With amendment to above direction on 03.12.2025, the parking spaces owned and
managed by DMRC, which provide essential public transport connectivity and park
and ride facilities, have been exempted from the doubling of parking charges.
5. Deployment of electric heaters for guards and RWAs: Direction u/s 5 of the
   Environment Protection Act, 1986 issued on 24.12.2025 whereby open burning of
   biomass, leaves, municipal solid waste, plastic, rubber, or any other combustible
   material, whether for heating or for any other purpose, is strictly prohibited and
   every resident Welfare Association (RWA), housing society, institution,
   government or private establishment, contractor, agency, or any other entity
   engaging or deploying staff for security, sanitation, horticulture, or other
   miscellaneous services shall be responsible for ensuring effective supervision,
   monitoring, and preventive control such as adequate heating arrangements (via
   electric/approved fuels) to ensure that no person so engaged, employed, or
   deployed under their authority or control indulges in any such prohibited open
   burning, failing which liability shall be attracted in accordance with applicable
   provision of law.

 6. Pilot project of cloud seeding/ artificial rain:
    It is proposed to conduct a trial of pilot project for implementation of Cloud Seeding
    as a measure to Combat Episodic High Air Pollution in Delhi, as a short-term
    emergency measure for artificial rainfall generation to disperse and reduce
    ambient air pollution levels. Delhi Cabinet has approved a pilot project on
    Technology Demonstration and Evaluation of Cloud Seeding as alternative for
    Delhi NCR Pollution Mitigation and the same will be undertaken in collaboration
    with IIT Kanpur, based on cloud forecast by IMD, after monsoon. DGCA has
    provided the clearance for the month of October – November 2025. MOU has been
    signed on 25th September 2025 between IIT Kanpur and Department of
    Environment, GNCTD. So far trials have been conducted on 23.10.25 and
    28.10.2025. Further trials will be conducted in consultation with IMD.

 7. Constitution of Expert Group and implementation Committee:
    Delhi continues to face severe and recurring episodes of air pollution due to
    multiple anthropogenic and natural factors. Addressing Air Pollution challenges
    requires a scientific, coordinated, and multi-sectoral strategy aligned with national
    frameworks, emerging technologies, and sector- specific interventions. To guide
    and support the Government of NCT of Delhi (GNCTD) in evidence-based
    decision-making, an “Expert Group on Air Pollution Mitigation” was constituted on
    06.12.2025. An Implementation Committee on Control of Air Pollution (ICCAP) also
    constituted vide separate order on 06.12.2025 to implement recommendations of
    Expert Group.

2.3.5    Implementation of National Clean Air Programme (NCAP)
   Delhi is part of National Clean Air Program (NCAP) launched by M/o Environment,
   Forest & Climate Change, Government of India, where a series of interventions in
   various sectors [transport/road dust/waste and biomass burning etc.] with respect
   to ambient air quality is being planned and implemented as part of air pollution
   mitigation measures. 40% reduction of Particulate Matter (PM10) concentration is
   being targeted by March 2026.

                                                  ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26     119

     Delhi (MCD) for the purchase of Mechanical Road Sweepers, Water Sprinkler/Anti-
     Smog Gun and Road patch repair machine/Pot hole repair machine under NCAP.
     MCD so far has utilized ₹ 13.41 Crores only for Procurement and Operation &
     Maintenance of 28 water Sprinklers. An amount of ₹8.93 Crores for FY 2023-24
     has been released to New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) for the End-to-End
     paving along the roads, Greening of traffic corridor and C&D waste management
     under NCAP. NDMC so far has utilized only ₹1.14 cr for air quality improvement.


2.4 Monitoring and Action against persons for burning of waste material /Garbage
   in open:

   2.4.1       Open burning of biomass and solid waste is another significant contributor
           to air pollution especially during winters. National Green Tribunal vide, its various
           orders in OA 21 of 2014 titled “Vardhman Kaushik Vs Union of India & Ors”,
           regarding air Pollution in Delhi has passed directions for controlling Air Pollution.

    1. National Green Tribunal vide its order dated 28th April, 2015 has imposed
       compensation on burning of any kind of garbage leaves, waste plastic, rubber,
       self-moulding compound and such other material in open as under:
       “the person who is found actually burning such material and/or responsible
       abating such burning would be liable to pay compensation in terms of Section 15
       of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 for polluting environment and would be
       liable to pay a sum of ₹5,000 to be paid instantaneously.”

    2. Dedicated 622 patrolling teams have been deployed for prevention of open
       burning during winter 2025. Anti–open burning drive had been launched in
       coordination with stakeholder departments.

    3. A detailed protocol is in place for controlling fire at landfill sites and as a result
       the numbers of landfill fires have come down from 159 in 2017 to 0 in 2025.

    4. The total legacy waste present at all three dumpsites in year 2019 was 280 Lakh
       MT and Municipal Corporation of Delhi has bio-mined 204.94 L a k h MT till
       16.11.2025. The timeline for 100% remediation of legacy waste is July 2026 for
       Okhla, December 2026 for Bhalswa & December 2027 for Ghazipur.

 2.6     Measures for road dust pollution control from roads & open areas:

2.6.1      Comprehensive Road Redevelopment Action Plan: As per direction
         from CAQM, a comprehensive road redevelopment action plan with a
         strategy to map all roads required to be re-developed and a detailed action
         plan as per framework for implementation of the paving and greening
         measures in Right of Way (RoW), with financial estimate had been prepared
         of ₹6,000 crore for comprehensive road improvement works. In Delhi total
         road length of about 3,300 km require resurfacing or improvement, this 3,300
         km inter alia include 800 km of PWD roads, 1,200 km of MCD roads, and
         1,000 km of roads in unauthorized colonies. The redevelopment will follow
         the CAQM framework with end-to-end paving and greening, greening of
         central verges, and end-to-end paving and greening of roads including
         broken areas in parks and road sides.


2.6.2     Plan to pave/green all Roadways/ Central verges:

         For ensuring no suspension of roadside dust, greening and paving of central
         verges and road sides is being undertaken by road owning and maintaining
         agency. As on 31.12.2025, 1071.86 kms of roadside has been paved and
         1093.91 km of central verges has been greened. Balance of 315.281 km
         roadside is targeted for paving and balance of 24.11 km of central verge is
         targeted to be greened by March 2026.

         Under NCAP, DPCC has also transferred ₹19.3375 crore to MCD for
         undertaking activities as per Annual Action Plan 2024–25. The funds are to be
         utilized for end-to-end paving of roads along with black-topping and
         maintaining potholes free roads and greening of traffic corridors, open areas,
         gardens, community places, schools and housing societies.

2.7      Electric vehicle augmentation and action against polluting vehicles:

2.7.1 Promotion of Electric Vehicles: To further improve Delhi’s air quality and
      create an entire supply-chain ecosystem for clean fuel/ electric vehicles, the
      Delhi Govt. will be notifying a policy, ‘Delhi Electric Vehicles Policy 2026’. The
      policy intends to strengthen EV adoption with effect from 01.04.2026 to
      31.03.2030. As on January 2026, Delhi has a total bus fleet of 5,525 buses,
      comprising 1,911 CNG and 3,614 electric buses, with plans to induct an
      additional 1,988 EV buses by March 2026 and 510 more by December 2026.

        Additionally, 2,800 E-DRIVE buses (DTC Allocation: 1,380 E-buses & Cluster
        Allocation - 1,420 E-Buses) are proposed to be inducted under the PM E-Drive
        scheme.

2.7.2    Imposition of charge on light and heavy-duty commercial vehicles
        entering Delhi: In compliance with the order dated 09.10.2015 and 16.12.2015
        of Hon’ble Supreme Court, Environment Compensation Charge (ECC) is levied
        on Delhi bound light and heavy-duty commercial goods vehicles. The Hon’ble
        Supreme Court of India has withdrawn the exemption on ECC that was allowed
        for commercial vehicles carrying essential goods (such as vegetables, fruits,
        milk, grains, eggs, poultry items, ice used for food and salt) to enter Delhi
        without paying the Environment Compensation Cess (ECC).

2.7.3 Returning of non-destined goods vehicles: Delhi Traffic Police ensure active
      cooperation with the toll plaza staff at border entry points for checking &
      returning of the goods vehicles not destined from Delhi, from the border entry
      points, in compliance to orders of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India.


2.7.4 Unauthorized Parking: Unauthorized parking leads to encroachments and
      reduces road capacity, causing traffic congestion and prolonged idling of
      vehicles. This results in increased vehicular emissions, contributing significantly
      to urban air pollution, particularly PM2.5 and NO2 levels. Hence constant vigil is
      maintained by Delhi Traffic Police to check & control unauthorized / improper
      parking of vehicles. The violators are booked under section 122/177 of the
      Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The vehicles found parked in obstructive manner are
      also towed away. Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) have been directed to develop
      and implement parking area management plan and parking pricing strategy.

2.7.5 Unauthorized entry of vehicles: Transport Dept., GNCT of Delhi and Delhi
      Traffic Police have imposed restriction on plying of goods vehicles on specified
      roads during specified timings such as 24 hrs. of the day, day time (7 AM to 11
      PM), peak hours (7 AM to 11 AM & 5 PM to 11 PM) etc. with an objective to
      decongest the roads and consequential impact on air pollution. The violators
      are booked under section 194(1)/115 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

                                                 ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26     123
2.7.6 Addressing the 62 traffic congestion points: Delhi Traffic Police has
      identified 62 congestion points across the city, of which 30 priority locations
      have been taken up for immediate corrective interventions. Definite timelines
      ranging from three months to one year have been fixed for structural
      improvements at the remaining locations. 222 traffic police personnel are
      deployed. Strengthened through deployment of 1,200 additional personnel
      provided by the Government of Delhi from the Delhi Transport Corporation.


2.7.7 End of Life Vehicles: As per latest order dated 17.12.2025, in the matter
      regarding phasing out of End-of-Life vehicles (10 years diesel and 15 years
      petrol) the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India has directed not to take coercive
      steps on grounds of age of the BS-IV and above vehicles while the matter is
      still sub-judice.

      now classified under 4 different stages of adverse air quality in Delhi as per revised

        GRAP I      :           POOR Category                   201-300
        GRAP II     :           VERY POOR Category              301-400

        GRAP III    :           SEVERE Category                 401-450

        GRAP IV      :          SEVERE + Category AQI            > 450

      Proactively implementing GRAP measures based on air quality forecasts, rather
      than retroactively implementing them once the acceptable levels are breached.

      Areas; and is reviewed regularly at the highest level. This year GRAP is being

2.10      To Control local Sources of Air Pollution at source
       13 Hotspots namely, Narela, Bawana, Mundka, Wazirpur, Rohini, R.K.Puram,
       Okhla, Jahangirpuri, Anand Vihar, Vivek Vihar, Punjabi Bagh, Ashok Vihar and
       Dwarka have been identified on the basis of Annual concentration of PM2.5 & PM10
       in Delhi. Specific action plans have been drawn up for identifying and mitigating
       the local sources of air pollution such as plastic & garbage, Malba / C&D waste
       removal, road patches and pot holes’ repair, De-congestion of congested traffic
       points, Mechanical road sweeping and Water sprinkling of roads, Closure of
       polluting & unauthorized industries, Night patrolling to check violations with
       respect to Bio-mass burning, C&D waste dumping etc., greenery development etc.

       Department of Environment and Delhi Pollution Control Committee has
       inventoried more than 5,857 pollution sources at 13 Hotspots and issues/
       complaints raised have been on-boarded on Green Delhi App for enabling online
       redressal by concerned department and monitoring. Re-Inventorisation of major
       point sources of air pollution in all identified hotspots in Delhi has been carried out.

       PWD had been directed to allocate Anti- Mobile Smog Guns (ASGs) specifically at
       all 13 hotspots for dust pollution control, with fund from Department of
       Environment.

    Terminal and Baba Kharak Singh Marg, Connaught Place. Smog Tower at
    Connaught Place was made operational for pilot studies w.e.f 01.09.2021. IIT
    Bombay had conducted the pilot study for the assessment of outdoor air
    purification system (Smog Tower) and submitted its final report on 05.10.2023. As
    per report submitted by IIT-Bombay the overall efficiencies are around 48- 56%
    for 20m; 34-30% for 21- 99m; 12-13% for 100-199m; 13% for 200-399m; 13-14%
    for greater than 400m, also it has been suggested that smog tower reduces 13%
    of air pollutants in 500m radius during the winter season. Smog tower was a pilot
    study to assess the performance of outdoor air purification system in ambient
    environment
a) Smog towers at Connaught place were found to have limited effectiveness that is
    i.e zone of influence of filtered air jet is too small to ensure the effectiveness and
    efficacy of smog tower.
b) Performance of CP tower overall average % reduction calculated by including all
    data collected for two years i.e 2021-2023.

2.12       Industrial pollution control:
  1.       Utilization of approved fuels:
         Implementation of Notification issued on Approved Fuel for Industries.
          Contribution by the industries to air pollution in National Capital Territory of
          Delhi is minimal compared to other sources. All the industries in National
          Capital Territory of Delhi, which have boiler/furnace, have been directed to
          convert to Piped Natural Gas (PNG).
         Out of 2049 industries, 1890 industries converted to Piped Natural Gas (PNG)
          and use of unapproved fuels is effectively checked to curb air pollution due
          to industrial emissions. 67 are running on approved fuel i.e. LPG and are in


                                                                                             1
                                                   ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26     127
         process of conversion to PNG too and the remaining 92 industries have
         moved out of Delhi.

  2.     Sealing of polluting industries:
        First-ever survey of polluting industries conducted in notified industrial areas,
         redevelopment areas and non-confirming areas in Delhi. Based on the
         surveys, over 700 air/ water polluting units in conforming areas have been
         sealed by DPCC and more than 300 air/water polluting units in non-
         conforming areas by MCD.

2.13 Bio-decomposer Technology to control Stubble burning and preventive
     measures:

       Institute of Agricultural and Research Institute (IARI) Pusa, has developed its
       own bio-decomposer technology for crop residue decomposition. In 2025-26,
       GNCTD has completed spraying of Bio decomposers in 3,655 A c r e s of non-
       basmati paddy agricultural fields at North, North-West, West, Central and
       South-West districts of Delhi. No case of stubble burning in Delhi has taken
       place in the present paddy harvesting season because of intense monitoring
       and awareness generated among paddy cultivators by the Development
       Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi. All (05) burning incidents reported by
       CREAM in October and November 2025 within Delhi Territory have been
       physically verified, and none of them constitute stubble or paddy residue
       burning. The monitoring reporting and preventive actions taken are as follows:

  a) Field Surveillance & Awareness: A total of 11 surveillance teams have been
     deployed round the clock across agricultural fields for continuous patrolling to
     prevent paddy residue burning and for conducting awareness drives among
     farmers.

  b) Pusa Bio-Decomposer Application: The Pusa Bio-Decomposer has been
     sprayed over 3655 acres of agricultural land for eco-friendly decomposition of
     paddy residue till now since 14.10.2025.
  c) Control Room: A dedicated Control Room has been operationalised in the
     Agriculture Unit for real-time monitoring of burning incidents and coordination
     of field teams.

  d) Custom Hiring Centers (CHCs): Two Custom Hiring Centers, one each in
     North-West and South-West Districts of Delhi, are under establishment to
     ensure farmer access to machinery for residue management.

  e) Demonstrations of Bio-Decomposer: A total of 97 demonstrations of the Pusa
     Bio-Decomposer in all the paddy cultivated area of Delhi have been conducted


                                                                                            1
 128        ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26
        to showcase effectiveness in residue decomposition and avoid the need for
        burning.

  f)    Farmer Training Programmes: Training programmes on paddy residue
        management have been conducted across districts covering all paddy growing
        farmers and educating them on sustainable and non-burning alternatives.

2.14    Use of IT for control of Pollution

   1. Green Delhi Application and Green War Room (GWR) for public
      grievance redressal: Govt. of Delhi launched Green Delhi App having 30
      agencies of Delhi on one platform. The grievances uploaded on Green Delhi.
      App is monitored through Green War Room. Further, the “Green Delhi” App
      was re-launched on 30th September 2024 for public grievances redressal.
      More than 1,00,840 complaints received through this app and resolution of
      more than 91% complaints is done.

   2. SAMEER App and social media: All the complaints received through
      SAMEER App and social media are dealt with proper care on a daily basis. All
      the complaints are forwarded to relevant departments timely and their
      resolution is monitored at the senior level.

   3. Dust Pollution Control Self-Assessment Web portal: DPCC developed a
      Dust Pollution Control Self-Assessment Web Portal for C&D projects on plot
      area 500sqm and more than 500sqm (dustcontroldpcc.delhi.gov.in) on
      01.10.2021 which was formally launched on 07.10.2021, in compliance to
      directions of Commission for Air Quality Management dated 11.06.2021.
      Training and hearings for the effective management of portal as well as dust
      mitigation measures to be undertaken at project sites has been provided to
      above 400 project proponents and 1730 no. of projects registered themselves
      on the portal till 07.01.2026.

3.     Noise Pollution

3.1 Delhi witnesses excessive noise on account use of high sound loudspeakers
    during festivals and many social gatherings in public place directly increases the
    noise pollution in the affected areas. GNCTD has notified an area of 100 meters
    around the hospitals with 100 beds or more, educational institutions with 1000
    students or more, all court complexes, all government complexes as Silence
    Areas/Zones. The Central Pollution Control Board published the information
    regarding permitted ambient noise levels in different areas. The prescribed
    ambient noise levels are as presented in Chart 8.3.

3.4     Noise limiter notification:

In compliance to Hon’ble National Green Tribunal directions; GNCTD issued Noise
limiter Notification on 21st November 2019 under sub-rule (3) of rule 3 and sub-rule (3)
of rule 5 read with clause (c) of rule 2 of the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control)
Rules, 2000, to ensure that no audio system or public address system shall be let out
/ installed without being fitted with Sound limiter in any function in the whole of National
Capital Territory of Delhi.

4.       WATER POLLUTION

4.1    The river Yamuna, the reason for Delhi’s existence, has suffered heavily from
Pollution which is due to the flow of untreated / partially treated sewage and Industrial
effluents.

         About 48 KM Stretch in Delhi from Palla to Badarpur (Delhi-Haryana border).
         About 26 KM Stretch from Wazirabad (Downside of Wazirabad Barrage) to
          Asgarpur Village (after Okhla Barrage), which is less than 2% of the river
          Length, accounts for about major pollution load in the river.
         22 Drains outfall into river Yamuna including waste water coming into Najafgarh
          Drain from Haryana and coming into Shahdara Drain from Uttar Pradesh.
         10 Cumecs of Water is being released by the State of Haryana at Hathanikund
          during lean season. However, most of it evaporates or percolates before it
          reaches Wazirabad during the lean season and therefore it is highly inadequate
          to meet the dilution requirement to achieve the desired water Quality of BOD<
          3 mg/l & DO >5 mg/l.

4.2     Water Quality of River Yamuna: Water quality of river Yamuna is monitored
by DPCC on monthly basis at 8 Locations i.e. Palla, Wazirabad, ISBT Bridge, ITO
Bridge, Nizamudin Bridge, Okhla Barrage, Agra Canal at Okhla Barrage, Asgarpur
(After confluence of Shahdara & Tuglakabad drains).
4.3     DPCC has been conducting monthly water quality monitoring of river Yamuna
(at 8 locations) and 27 drains including 2 drains (Indrapuri & Sahibabad Drains coming
from Uttar Pradesh) discharging waste water into river Yamuna.

4.4  The highest average of DO is 7.4 mg/l at Palla and lowest is 1.6 mg/l at River
Yamuna at Asgarpur (After confluence of Shahdara & Tuglakabad drains).

4.5     Water quality monitoring results of the drains indicate that most of the drains
still have to meet the standards with respect to Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD),
Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) and Total Suspended Solids (TSS).

unauthorized colonies. Coverage of sewerage network in NCT of Delhi is about 82%
and remaining 18% area (mainly unauthorized colonies and JJ clusters) is unsewered.
There are 1799 Unauthorized Colonies in Delhi. DJB has provided Timelines for laying
sewerage network in unauthorized colonies not having sewerage system.

4.10    Interceptor Sewer Project (ISP)

       Delhi Jal Board initiated the process of laying of interceptor sewers along 3
major drains (Najafgarh Drain, Supplementary Drain and Shahdara Drain) for trapping
of 108 sub drains out falling into these drains. About 242 MGD of sewage generated
from the colonies/ other sources & coming through the 108 sub drains will be trapped
before reaching the above-mentioned major drains and the same would be diverted to
the existing underutilized STPs / New STPs for treatment of sewage. Treatment of 242
MGD of sewage as planned will take place after construction / rehabilitation of
Coronation Pillar & Rithala and Kondli STP under YAP-III.

4.13      Sewage and Fecal Sludge Management (Septage Management)

Delhi Water Board Septage Management Regulation 2018 were notified by the Urban
Development Department, GNCTD on 12.11.2018 (published in Gazette on
21.11.2018) and necessary action is to be taken by Delhi Jal Board, District
Magistrates and Local Bodies / Municipal Corporations as per the provisions of the
said Notification.

Urban Development Department, GNCTD has issued “Delhi Water Board Septage
Management (Amendment) Regulation, 2024” on 13.03.2024 including following
amendments in the existing Regulations:

1.        (a) Penalty for deposit of septage by unauthorized (unlicensed) entities shall be
          ₹ 50,000/- plus confiscation of vehicle.

(b)       Penalty for disposal of Septage at places other than the designated places by
          authorized licensee shall be ₹ 50,000/- per violation.
(c)       Penalty on a person who uses the services of unlicensed vendors/vehicles for
          discharging the septage shall be ₹ 10,000/- per violation.

2.        An officer not lower than the rank of Naib Tehsildar in DM offices, JE in
          DJB/I&FC, Sub Inspector in Delhi Police and Sanitary Inspector in CD shall be
          competent to impose penalty.

Installation of GPS System - Each Vehicle used for transportation of septage shall
be fitted with GPS device and access rights of the movement data shall be given to
the Delhi Jal Board for tracking of such vehicles.

DJB has registered 164 licensed vendors (Emptiers) for collection and transportation
of sewage from the septic tanks and has identified 86 designated SPS/ STPs for
receiving the Septage.

given in following Table:

4.14     Prevention of Dumping of Solid Waste in Drains and River Yamuna

For preventing the dumping of solid waste in the drains, all the concerned
Departments/ Agencies have been directed vide order dated 09.01.2019 of Chief
Secretary and Order dated 15.01.2019 of UD Department, GNCTD for taking
necessary action against the violators including imposition of Environmental
Compensation of ₹5000 on dumping of Pooja Material/ Flowers etc. and ₹ 50,000 on
the dumping of Construction Material / Malba in River Yamuna.


4.15 Protection of Flood Plain of River Yamuna

As per the orders of Hon’ble NGT dated 13.01.2015, Flood Plain of River Yamuna is
to be protected, Unauthorized Habitation/ Settlements/ Encroachment are to be
removed by DDA and cultivation of Edible Crops are prohibited. Following action has
been / is being taken by DDA for protection of Flood Plain of river Yamuna and
prevention of Encroachment:

Demarcation of Flood plain and Removal of Illegal Encroachments:

       (a) Demarcation of 1 in 100 years Flood Plains & Fixing up of Bollards
       (b) Engagement of Private Security to stop illegal Dumping
       (c) Installation of Electronic Surveillance System
       (d) Removal of Encroachment from the Flood Plain
       (e) Demolition Program
       (f) Removal of C&D Waste
       (g) Restoration and Rejuvenation of the Floodplains of River Yamuna.

4.17 Ban on Idol Immersion

DPCC issued Directions under Section 33A of the Water (Prevention and Control of
Pollution) Act, 1974 on 26.08.2025, prohibiting idol immersion in the River Yamuna
and allowing only eco-friendly, earthen idols for Durga Puja, Ganesh Utsav, and other
festivals. The Department of Environment published awareness advertisements in



                                                                                        1
 144        ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26
national dailies, and the District Administration created designated temporary
immersion sites to facilitate eco-friendly practices and prevent pollution.

4.19    High Level Committee (HLC) for Rejuvenation of River Yamuna

       As per the directions of the Hon’ble NGT in OA No. 673 / 2018 Dated 20.09.2018,
       polluted river stretches are to be rejuvenated at least for bathing purpose with
       quality of river as given below:

             Quality Parameter                      Standards to be Achieved

             BOD                                    ˂ 3 mg/l

             Dissolved Oxygen (DO)                  > 5.0 mg/l.

             Faecal Coliform                        <500 MPN/100ml.


       The matter related to control of pollution in river Yamuna is being monitored by
       Chief Secretary through various meetings. Urban Development Department,
       Govt. of NCT of Delhi vide order dated 22.05.2025 has constituted a committee
       headed by Chief Secretary, GNCTD to work upon Yamuna River under the
       project called “Urban River Management Plan (URMP).


       Vide order dated 02.07.2025, Urban Development Department, Govt. of NCT of
       Delhi has constituted High Level Committee (HLC) for Rejuvenation of River
       Yamuna under the Chairpersonship of Hon’ble Chief Minister, Hon’ble Minister
       (Water), is Co-Chairperson and Chief Secretary of GNCTD is Convener of HLC.
       Secretary Ministry of Jal Shakti and Secretary, Ministry of Housing & Urban
       Affairs (MoHUA), Government of India and HODs of various Departments /
       Organisations are members in the HLC, Secretary, CEO, DJB is Member
       Secretary / Nodal Officer of HLC. The HLC will oversee and guide the
       rejuvenation of Yamuna River in Delhi ensuring a comprehensive and
       sustainable approach to restore its ecological health and aesthetic value.
       Vide another order dated 02.07.2025, issued by the Urban Development
       Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi, an Executive Committee for Rejuvenation
       of River Yamuna under the chairmanship of Chief Secretary, GNCTD has been
       constituted for execution of the directions of above mentioned of HLC Chaired
       by Hon’ble Chief Minister, Delhi.

(a)         Municipal Solid Waste Processing and Disposal Facilities

           There is one Integrated Solid Waste Management Facility at Bawana for
           processing of 2000 TPD of municipal solid waste having Waste to Energy Plant,
           Compost Plant and Engineered Sanitary Landfill. One Engineered Sanitary
           Landfill of MCD has been commissioned at Tehkhand on 12.03.2024.



(b)         Waste to Energy Plants

           Delhi has 4 Waste to Energy Plants (WTE Plants) of capacity 6550 TPD at 4
           different locations in Delhi namely Okhla, Ghazipur, Bawana and Tehkhand. One
           new Waste to Energy Plant of capacity of 3000 TPD was proposed at Narela-
           Bawana. Public Hearing of the said proposed plant at Narela-Bawana was held
           on 27.12.2024. Environment Clearance (EC) accorded by MoEFCC on
           18.06.2025. The 03 numbers of 400 KV transmission lines have to be shifted from
           the proposed sites. Necessary payment of shifting amounting to Rs 23.27 crore
           has been made to power grid on 19.06.2025. Work of shifting of transmission

i.       The legacy waste remediation activity being implemented by the Urban
         Development Department, GNCTD, at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla dumpsites
         has demonstrated steady progress since the baseline assessment of 203 lakh
         metric tonnes (LMT) established through a drone survey in June 2022. The
         interventions undertaken over successive financial years indicate a clear shift
         towards systematic reduction of accumulated waste. A distinct improvement is
         observed in FY 2025–26 (April 2025 to February 2026), which marks the most
         substantial progress to date. During this period, 74.11 LMT of legacy waste has
         been remediated, representing the highest annual processing achieved so far.
         This accelerated pace has resulted in a sharp reduction of the balance quantity
         to 120.82 LMT, even after accounting for 30.74 LMT of fresh waste disposed
         during the same period. The magnitude of reduction achieved within a single year
         highlights a marked strengthening of execution capacity and operational
         efficiency. The data reflects that the remediation programme has entered a phase
         of accelerated impact, with the most recent year contributing significantly to
         overall reduction in legacy waste. Bhalswa and Okhla dumpsites continue to
         show substantial decline in pending waste, while Ghazipur has also registered
         steady progress. The deployment of 62 trommels across the three sites has
         supported this enhanced performance by augmenting processing capacity and
         enabling sustained operations.

5.4     Electronic Waste

5.4.1     As per the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, which came into effect on 1st
        April 2023, entities falling under the categories of Manufacturer, Producer,
        Refurbisher and Recycler are required to register on the Central Pollution Control
        Board (CPCB) Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) portal. There is no such
        recycling facility in Delhi. Only Bulk Consumers are being pursued for disposal of
        e-waste, through scientific manner by having MoU/Agreement with CPCB
        registered recyclers.



5.4.2    3 Dismantlers and 13 Refurbishes have been issued consent/authorization by
        DPCC as per E-Waste rules and CPCB guidelines.

5.4.3    The Government of NCT of Delhi, through DSIIDC as the executing agency, is
        developing an E-waste Eco Park in Holambi Kalan to manage E-waste in the
        region. M/s E&Y Co. LLP was appointed as the Project Management Consultant
        (PMC) via an open E-tender and their preliminary report was approved by the
        Steering Committee on 13.12.2023. The Eco Park will be developed on a PPP
        model, and a request to change the land use from residential to utility has been
        submitted to DDA. Land for establishing the E-Waste Eco Park at Holambi
        Kalan has been allotted by DDA to the Department of Environment. MoHUA,

5.5     Plastic Waste
       The plastic menace poses a significant environmental challenge in Delhi, with
       single-use plastics contributing heavily to pollution and health risks for humans,
       animals, and plants. Globally, single-use plastics, made primarily from fossil
       fuels, account for one-third of all plastic produced. India has completely banned
       single-use plastics, with penalties of up to ₹15 lakh or imprisonment for violations
       under the Environment Protection Act, 1986.

       Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 as amended in 2018 issued by
       MoEF& CC, GOI
       The rules cast responsibilities on various stakeholders including generators,
       producers, Urban Local Bodies, Urban Development Department, Local
       Administration and the Pollution Control Board/ Committee.

5.6 Ban on Single-Use Plastics

       As per Condition No. 4(2)(a & b) of the Plastic Waste Management (Amendment)
       Rules, 2021 (notified on 12.08.2021), the manufacture, import, stocking,
       distribution, sale and use of 19 specified single-use plastic items— including
       plastic sticks (earbuds, balloons, flags, candy, ice-cream), polystyrene/thermocol
       for decoration, and items such as plates, cups, glasses, cutlery, straws, trays,
       wrapping films for sweet boxes, invitation cards and cigarette packets,
       plastic/PVC banners below 100 microns, and stirrers (except compostable
       plastic)—stand prohibited from 1st July 2022.

                                                    ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26   155
      Action Taken by Department of Environment to eliminate Single Use Plastic
      & to promote alternatives to SUPs in Delhi:

      Special Task Force: Department of Environment, Government of National
      Capital Territory of Delhi constituted the Special Task Force under the
      Chairmanship of Chief Secretary, Delhi which is reviewing the implementation of
      PWM rules and making efforts for eliminating single use plastic from Delhi.

      Information, Education and Communication (IEC) Plan: IEC plan for different
      stakeholders was prepared for execution by all stakeholder departments
      including education, Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), Department of Environment,
      Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) etc.

      Advisory on phasing out SUP items: The Advisory on phasing out SUP items
      was issued dated 28th Feb, 2025 for government offices of Govt. of NCT of Delhi.
      Department of Environment requested to the Directorate of Education and
      Directorate of Training & Technical Education, GNCTD to initiate and give wider
      publicity among school & college students.

      Training and Sensitization Programmes on Single Use Plastics and Plastic
      Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2022:

      Various training and sensitization programmes were conducted with ULBs, Eco-
      Clubs (schools and colleges), the Revenue Department, DPCC enforcement
      teams, and Market Traders’ Associations from April 2025 to December 2025.
      Under the EEP Scheme of MoEF&CC, the Department of Environment
      organised multiple workshops through Eco-Club schools during the current FY.
      Additionally, a sensitization programme was assigned to TERI to sensitize school
      and college students on biodiversity, climate change, and prevention of plastic
      pollution.



      The Government of Delhi imposed a ban on the manufacture, sale, storage,
      use, import, and transport of all plastic carry bags in the NCT of Delhi vide
      Notification dated 23.10.2012. This notification was challenged before the
      Hon’ble Delhi High Court by the All India Plastic Industries Association (WPC
      7012/2012). On 05.12.2016, the Hon’ble High Court transferred the matter to
      the Hon’ble NGT, which, through an interim order dated 10.08.2017, directed
      a complete prohibition on the use of non-compostable plastic carry bags of
      less than 50 microns, along with an Environmental Compensation of ₹5,000
      per violation. Subsequent amendments to the PWM Rules, 2022 permitted
      plastic carry bags of more than 120 microns thickness across India.

       6.   Climate Change Mitigation Measures

  6.1       In order to address the challenges of climate change, Delhi Government has
            finalized Delhi Climate Change Action Plan which is aligned with National action
            plan on climate change.

 6.2        Following sectors have been identified as critical to the impact of climate change
            and comprehensive strategies have been drawn in State action plan on climate
            change.

            a)    Enhanced Energy Efficiency
            b)    Sustainable Habitat
            c)    Green India
            d)    Water Mission
            e)    Strategic Knowledge
            f)    Solar Mission

6.3         Department of Environment has engaged Deutsche Gesellschaft fur International

                                                                                           1
      158        ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26
              Zusammenarbeit (GIZ-India) for the revision of State Action Plan on Climate
              Change Delhi (SAPCC) as per the common framework guidelines for Revision
              of SAPCC provided by MoEF&CC, GOI. Revision of State Action Plan on Climate
              Change (SAPCC) for Delhi is in alignment with India’s Nationally Determined
              Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, the Sustainable Development
              Goals (SDGs), and prevalent national policies and missions. Revised SAPCC
              also known as SAPCC 2.0 outlines key initiatives and strategies reflecting our
              state's commitments and proposed actions to address climate change
              vulnerabilities across key identified sectors, including Energy. Urban Planning,
              Water Resources, Forests and Biodiversity, Transport, Health, Agriculture and
              Horticulture. It envisions a sustainable, inclusive, and climate-resilient low-
              carbon development pathway, with a focus on both adaptation and mitigation,
              while ensuring the protection of vulnerable communities from the adverse effects
              of climate change. The SAPCC 2.0 has been finalized, approved by the Delhi
              Government, and submitted to MoEF&CC for final approval.

7.            Green Delhi App

     7.1     Green Delhi app has been developed for information, awareness and redressal
             of grievances of the citizens at single platform. Govt. of Delhi launched Green
             Delhi App having 30 agencies of Delhi on one platform. The grievances uploaded
             on Green Delhi App are monitored through Green War Room. Further, the
             “Green Delhi” App developed by Department of Environment and Forests. More
             than 1,00,840 complaints received through this app and resolution of more than
             91% complaints is done.
           For efficient functioning of the GWR, the following five stakeholders are
           responsible:

           1. In charge GWR: to carry out overall operation of the GWR.
           2. DPCC Trainees: to carry out day to day operation of GWR.
           3. Nodal officers of Agencies: for timely resolution of complaints within their
              Departments.
           4. DPCC Engineers: Cell In charge(s) of DPCC are responsible for taking action
              on the complaints including imposing EDC on the agencies responsible for
              redressal of complaints, in case of default.
           5. Green Delhi App IT Team (DPCC): Responsible to manage Green Delhi App
              Dashboard and other IT requirements of the GWR.

 9          FOREST IN DELHI
9.1    Delhi has the unique distinction as the greenest city in the country with 25.04% of
       total geographical area of the state under Green Cover (India State of Forest
       Report, 2023). The Delhi government is making sustained efforts to enhance the
       green cover in Delhi with aim to maintain a balance between ecology and
       development.

                                                                                         1
  160          ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26
9.2   As per Champion and Seth classification the forest types of Delhi fall broadly into
      two groups: (i) 5B/C2 Northern dry mixed deciduous forest and (ii) 6B/C2 Ravine
      thorn forest. The vegetation of Delhi is thorny scrub, which is found in the arid and
      semi-arid zone
9.3   The green cover of Delhi is increasing year after year on the lines of National
      Forest Policy, 1988 which stipulates that a minimum of 1/3rd of the total land area
      of the country should be under forest or tree cover. Taking the above in view, the
      Govt. of NCT of Delhi is making all endeavors to meet the national goal as set by
      the Central Govt. and is constantly adding to the green cover of the State
      Government. As a result of the initiatives taken by the Government of NCT of Delhi,
      forest and tree cover area has been increasing since last ten years which is
      reflected in the change in forest and tree cover given in statement 8.8:

10.    Water Conservation by Wetland Authority of Delhi

10.1 The Wetland Authority of Delhi was constituted on 23rd April 2019 under the
     Department of Environment and Forests, GNCTD. The Authority in coordination
     with sixteen water body owning agencies

10.2 Inventorisation and reconciliation of 1040 water bodies in Delhi is completed
     through coordination with 17 water body owning agencies.

10.3          Seven Districts has been identified model ponds (North, North West,
       South, South West, New Delhi, North East and West). Bench marks for Model
       Ponds prepared and sent to all District Magistrates by Wetland Authority of
       Delhi.

10.4 Brief Documents in prescribed format of Ministry of Environment Forest and
     Climate Change, Government of India, is a statutory requirement under
     Wetland Rules, 2017. This crucial document which contains ecological


                                                                                        1
                                                 ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26   165
         attributes and management challenges of the water body has been prepared in
         respect of 685 water bodies of Delhi.

  10.5 Hon’ble NGT had directed preparation of action plans for restoration of all
       wetlands. These action plans which propose conservation actions to be done in
       each water body have been completed in respect of 685 water bodies.

  10.6 Citizen engagement and public participation in the conservation of wetlands is
       planned through declaring wetland mitras, who can assist the authority in
       protection and restoration of wetlands.

  10.7 In pursuance of Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 a
       Technical Committee under Chairmanship of Dr. Madhu Verma, Chief
       Economist at the World Resources Institute at Delhi consisting of six wetland
       experts formed on 01.07.2021.

10.8 In pursuance of Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 a
     “Grievance Committee under Wetland Authority of Delhi was constituted on
     01.07.2021 as a mechanism for hearing and forwarding grievances raised by the
     public to the Wetland Authority on Wetlands falling under their respective
     jurisdiction.

10.9 The future plan of the Wetland Authority is to prepare a protocol for catchment
     area management, evolving low-cost restoration techniques, and actively engage,
     coordinate and help land owning agencies to prioritize wetlands based on the brief
     documents prepared and notify them, thus ensuring long term protection and
     conservation of wetlands in Delhi.
 10.10    Fire Prone Forest Classes
          Geographical area GNCTD having only less fire prone forest cover of
          197.67 sq km including scrub (ISFR 2023).

 11. Asola Bhatti Wild Life Sanctuary

 11.1    Asola Bhatti Wildlife Sanctuary is located in South Delhi, close to Tughlakabad
         Fort. The Wildlife Sanctuary harbors diverse flora and fauna and offers a vital
         green space in the city. It was founded in 1992 with the purpose to safeguard
         the wildlife in the area between Delhi and Surajkund (Delhi-Haryana border).
         The Southern Ridge's legal status was deemed unclear until 1986, when the
         villages of Asola, Sahurpur and Maidangari received notification of their
         community land (2679.29 acres), followed by notifications of the land of Bhatti
         village area (2166.28 acres) in 1991 and the land of Tughlakabad village area
         (29.64 acres) in 1992.




                                                                                      1
   166      ECONOMIC SURVEY OF DELHI, 2025-26
11.2   Asola Bhatti Wildlife Sanctuary is home to a diverse range of flora and fauna.
       The sanctuary is known for its rich avian diversity, with over 200 species of birds
       recorded, including the Indian Peafowl, Eurasian thick-knee, and Indian Eagle-
       Owl. During winters, the Neeli Jheel is visited by migratory species such black-
       winged stilts and tufted ducks. Asola Bhati is home to several mammals such
       as the Indian Leopard (Panthera Pardus), Striped Hyena (Hyeana Hyeana),
       Nilgai (Boselaphys Tragocamelus), Golden Jackal (Canis Aureus), and Indian
       Porcupine (Hystrix Indica). Camera trapping studies have helped identify at
       least 8 resident leopards in the sanctuary. Reptiles like the Bengal Monitor
       Lizard (Varanus Bengalensis), Indian Rock Python (Python Molarus), Indian
       Cobra (Naja Naja), Leopard Gecko (Eublepharis Macularius) can be found here
       as well. Asola Bhatti's varied habitats, includes scrubland, grassland, and rocky
       terrain which support the rich biodiversity, making it a valuable conservation
       area amidst the urban landscape of Delhi.

11.3 The Forest Department has enhanced eco-tourism at the sanctuary. Visitors
     can immerse themselves in the sanctuary's diverse habitats, while encountering
     a rich variety of flora and fauna. The Neeli Jheel is an ideal peaceful retreat
     offering birding and nature gazing space. Nature walking trails, cycling tracks
     and Conservation Education Centre have been functioning to help the visitors
     make their visit both fun and educational. The Asola Bhati Butterfly Park,
     inhabited by a variety of butterflies such as the common Pierot, Red Pierot,
     Danaid Eggfly, Blue Pansy etc. Three nurseries growing a wide variety of plants
     ranging from fruiting, medicinal to aesthetics and flowering ones have been
     developed at Asola Bhati.


11.4 The sanctuary's serene surroundings provide a perfect solace from city life,
     making it an ideal destination for nature enthusiasts and eco-conscious
     travelers seeking to connect with Delhi's natural heritage while contributing to
     its preservation.

12.    Major Achievements of F.Y 2025-26:

12.1 The Department of Forests and Wildlife, GNCTD is working actively to increase
     and protect the green cover and the wildlife of the city state. To increase the
     green cover of the State, annual plantation drives are being carried out every
     year under Green Action Plan (GAP). GAP is implemented by Department of
     Forests and Wildlife, Govt. of NCT of Delhi, being the Nodal Agency in
     collaboration with more than 20 other Greening Agencies of the State. Every
     year the target for annual Green Action Plan is decided after consultation with
     all the Greening agencies.

12.2 During 2024-25 the Department of Forest and Wildlife, Govt. of NCT of Delhi with
      other greening agencies have planted 57.55 lakh saplings (including plantation
      of 13.48 lakh trees, 37.56 lakh shrubs and 6.51 lakh bamboos and free
      distribution of 10.43 lakh seedlings) against the plantation and distribution target
      of 64.14 lakh saplings.

12.3 During the Green Action Plan (GAP) 2025-26, the Department of Forests and
     Wildlife (GNCTD), in collaboration with 21 greening agencies, achieved a
     significant milestone by planting 53.70 lakh saplings as of January 2026. This
     achievement comprises 4.81 lakh trees, 41.82 lakh shrubs, and 2.03 lakh
     bamboos, complemented by the strategic distribution of 5.03 lakh seedlings to
     the public.

      (SOP) for tree felling/transplantation was issued. On 02.05.2025, the SOP for

        organised a month-long plantation campaign for Van Mahotsav 2025, launched
        by the Hon’ble Chief Minister on July 3rd at the Central Ridge. A key achievement
        was large-scale exhibition at Bharat Mandapam featuring 25 nurseries stalls and
        72 specialized stalls, with participation from renowned organizations like WWF
        and TERI.

        (ii) From July 5–31, the Department organized daily thematic plantation drives
         across 14 locations, involving Hon’ble Ministers, MPs, MLAs, and the general
         public. A major highlight was the VVIP plantation drive at PBG Polo Ground,
         where the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India and other judges of Hon’ble Supreme
         Court and Delhi High Court, and members of the NGT participated in the “Ek
         Ped Maa Ke Naam” initiative. Through the strategic involvement of religious
         institutions, Padma awardees, and business leaders, the Department
         successfully institutionalized the plantation drive as a comprehensive state-wide
         movement.

        plantation drive with participation of diplomats from 71 countries. The event was
        attended by Hon’ble Union Minister Shri Bhupender Yadav, Hon’ble Chief
        Minister Smt. Rekha Gupta, and Hon’ble Environment Minister Sh. Sardar
        Manjinder Singh Sirsa, underscoring India’s global sustainability goals.

                   INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT
Industrial development in the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi is moving away
from traditional chimneys toward “smart” production and characterized by a strategic
shift from traditional heavy manufacturing to a sophisticated, service-oriented, and
high technology ecosystem through knowledge-based, IT/ITeS, and small-scale
sectors, driven by its service economy, trade hub status, and focus on sustainable,
clean growth.

Delhi State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation (DSIIDC) is
developing modern estates and flatted factories, aiming for "walk-to-work"
environments and supporting skill development. Delhi is one of the largest centers for
small industries in the country, manufacturing a diverse range of goods including
textiles, automobile parts, electronics, and software. This Sector has a proven vast
potential to play a leading role in the overall development of the national economy.
Delhi has a service-led economy, strong in professional, IT, and trade services with
majorly focus on frontier technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI), robotics,
biotechnology, and green energy. Industrial policy promotes high-tech, knowledge-
based, and non-polluting industries.


1.    Growth statistics:

       Delhi comes under Front Runner category in the country in SDG i.e.,
        “SDG India Index and Dashboard 2023-24”as per NITI Aayog.

       Good progress under the Business Reform Action Plan scheme came
        under “Emerging Business Ecosystems category” in 2022.

       In the Logistics Ease Across Different States (LEADS) 2024 report, Delhi
        was recognized in the ‘Achievers’ Category among the Union Territories

2.    Infrastructure Details:

       Infrastructure and institutional setup is created & redeveloped through
        redevelopment of conforming and non-conforming industrial areas
        through Delhi State Industrial & Infrastructure Development Corporation
        Limited (DSIIDC) & Delhi Development Authority (DDA) in some of the
        industrial areas across the City.

       There are 29 planned Industrial Areas and 4 flatted factory complexes in
        Delhi. Additionally, the Government of India and State Government
        have notified 27 non-conforming industrial/godown clusters for
        redevelopment as per norms for redevelopment mentioned in MPD-
        2021/ draft MPD-2041.

          persons were employed in 8.75 lakh establishments with an average of 3.45
          employees per establishment. Out of the total, 0.9% persons were
          employed in rural areas, whereas, 99.1% were engaged in urban areas of
          Delhi. 8.05 % of the total establishments were managed by women
          entrepreneurs.
